title: Best Ducted Dehumidifier (2026): HVAC & Furnace-Mounted Picks
h1: The Best Ducted Dehumidifiers for Your HVAC System
dek: Your air conditioner was never meant to be your only line of defense against sticky summers. A dehumidifier tied into the ductwork quietly fixes the whole house at once.
description: The best ducted dehumidifiers that connect to your HVAC system or sit beside the furnace, compared on capacity, coverage, install style and efficiency.
intro: A **ducted dehumidifier** — often called an HVAC dehumidifier or furnace dehumidifier — mounts next to your air handler and pulls damp air from the return side of the ductwork, dries it, and hands it back to the system to deliver to every room. Instead of a portable humming in one corner with a bucket to empty, you get one quiet machine in the basement or utility closet, a permanent drain line and an even humidity level from the bedrooms to the back hall.

It's a bigger purchase than a portable, and it usually needs a contractor. But in humid climates, in tight newer homes, and in houses where the air conditioner is oversized and short-cycles without ever drying the air, adding a dehumidifier to the HVAC is often the single most effective comfort upgrade you can make. We compared the leading whole-home units on rated capacity, coverage, installation flexibility, efficiency, warranty and owner-reported reliability.
topPicksLead: For most homes with forced-air heating and cooling, the **Aprilaire E100** is the ducted dehumidifier to beat: high capacity, top-tier efficiency and a design HVAC installers know well.

products.whyWeLoveIt: The E100 is the unit HVAC pros reach for most often, and for good reason. It's built to connect to existing ductwork, it handles homes up to roughly 5,500 square feet, and it can run off its own control or a compatible thermostat so humidity is managed alongside temperature.
products.performance: Its 100-pint rating is measured under AHAM conditions (80°F, 60% humidity), which is the standard for whole-house equipment. The ENERGY STAR Most Efficient designation puts it among the lowest-cost units to run per pint removed, which matters for a machine that may log hundreds of hours a season. Owners commonly report steady 45–50% humidity throughout the house once it's dialed in; complaints tend to center on installation quality rather than the unit itself.
products.notes: If you also want the option of using it as a stand-alone basement unit later, the E100's freestanding mode gives you that flexibility. See all four models in our [best Aprilaire dehumidifier](/best/best-aprilaire-dehumidifier/) guide.

products.whyWeLoveIt: If your home is unusually large, leaky or in a very humid climate, the E130 gives you headroom the E100 can’t. It’s the same proven Aprilaire design scaled up, and the kind of dedicated ducted machine a local HVAC contractor can install and support for years.
products.performance: Rated at 130 pints a day under AHAM conditions with coverage up to about 7,400 square feet, the E130 suits large custom homes, homes with big finished basements and properties near the coast. Flexible control placement — on top or on the inlet side — helps in cramped mechanical rooms, and Aprilaire sells a Wi-Fi version, the E130W, if you want app control. Because dehumidifiers are sized on moisture load rather than floor area, have a contractor check your actual load before choosing it over the E100.
products.notes: Ask the installer which control strategy they plan to use — a dedicated dehumidistat, or a thermostat with humidity control — before you sign the quote.

blocks.text: That middle number matters when you shop. Whole-house units are rated under warmer, more humid AHAM conditions than the 65°F test used for portables since 2019, so their pint figures aren't directly comparable. A 70-pint ducted unit and a 50-pint portable are not as far apart as the labels suggest — our [dehumidifier size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/) explains the two rating systems.

We don't run a lab or install equipment in test houses. Instead we compare what's comparable: AHAM capacity ratings, ENERGY STAR listings, manufacturer installation manuals (duct sizes, airflow, drain and electrical requirements), warranty terms and recall history. Then we read owner reviews and contractor forums for recurring patterns — failed condensate pumps, coil leaks, noisy blowers, poor control integration.

For this guide we weighted three things most heavily: whether the unit is genuinely designed to connect to ductwork, how efficiently it removes water, and whether local HVAC contractors can realistically install and service it.

sections.heading: What to look for in an HVAC dehumidifier

items.label: Capacity matched to the house
items.text: Roughly 70–80 pints for an average home in a humid climate, 90–100 for larger or leakier houses, and more for very large homes. Our [best 100-pint dehumidifier](/best/best-100-pint-dehumidifier/) guide covers the top end.

items.label: Install configuration
items.text: Check that the unit supports the layout your installer recommends — return-to-return, return-to-supply, or a dedicated return.
sub: Return-to-return is the simplest and works with most systems
Return-to-supply lets the unit run without the furnace blower, which can save energy
Dedicated return pulls air from one damp area, such as a basement

items.label: Efficiency rating
items.text: Look for an ENERGY STAR or Most Efficient listing. A ducted unit can run hundreds of hours a summer, so efficiency shows up on the power bill. Our [ENERGY STAR dehumidifier](/best/best-energy-efficient-dehumidifier/) guide has more.

items.label: Controls that talk to your thermostat
items.text: A wall-mounted dehumidistat or a thermostat with humidity control keeps the system from fighting itself. Our [humidistat settings guide](/guides/dehumidifier-humidistat-settings-guide/) covers sensible targets.

items.label: A real drain plan
items.text: Ducted units drain continuously. Plan a gravity line to a floor drain or condensate pump before installation day.

items.label: Warranty and local support
items.text: Five to six years is typical. Ask whether the installer services the brand they're quoting.

blocks.text: Partly. An air conditioner removes moisture as a side effect of cooling, because warm, humid air condenses on the cold evaporator coil. The trouble is that it only dehumidifies while it's actively cooling. In spring and fall, on mild rainy days, or at night when the thermostat is satisfied, the AC sits idle while humidity creeps up. Oversized systems make it worse: they cool the house quickly and shut off before the coil has had time to pull much water out.

That's why so many homes feel cool but clammy. A dedicated HVAC dehumidifier fills the gap, drying the air whether or not the house needs cooling. Our explainer on [dehumidifier vs. air conditioner](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-air-conditioner/) goes deeper into the difference.

blocks.title: Before you buy
blocks.text: If your system is new and variable-speed, ask your contractor whether its built-in dehumidify mode is enough first. If humidity still sits above 55% on mild days, a ducted dehumidifier is the fix.

sections.heading: Adding a dehumidifier to your HVAC: what's involved

items: **Sizing.** A contractor estimates your moisture load from square footage, climate, insulation and any known wet spots like a basement or crawl space.
**Mounting.** The unit is set on a platform or hung near the furnace or air handler, with clearance for service.
**Ducting.** Inlet and outlet ducts are tied into the return and/or supply trunks, usually with a backdraft damper.
**Drainage.** A condensate line runs to a floor drain or a condensate pump.
**Power and controls.** The unit plugs into or is wired to a nearby circuit, and a dehumidistat or compatible thermostat is connected.

If your home feels sticky even with the AC running, a ducted dehumidifier is the permanent fix. The **Aprilaire E100** is the best all-around choice for most forced-air homes, the **Aprilaire E130** gives big or very humid homes extra headroom, and the **Santa Fe Ultra V100** is the pick for tight new construction that also needs fresh air. faqs.a: It's a whole-house dehumidifier that connects to your home's HVAC ductwork, usually beside the furnace or air handler. It pulls air from the return duct, removes moisture and sends the dried air back through the system to every room.

faqs.q: Can you add a dehumidifier to an existing HVAC system?
faqs.a: Yes. Most whole-house units are designed to be added to an existing forced-air system. A contractor ties the unit into the return (and sometimes supply) ducts, runs a condensate drain and connects a control. Homes without ductwork can use a freestanding whole-house unit or a portable instead.

faqs.q: Is a furnace dehumidifier the same as a whole-house dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Furnace dehumidifier is a common name for a whole-house unit mounted next to the furnace. The dehumidifier is a separate appliance; it simply shares the furnace's ductwork and blower to distribute dry air.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to add a dehumidifier to HVAC?
faqs.a: Most homeowners pay roughly $2,000–$4,500 installed, including a unit in the 70–130-pint range and professional labor. Complex installs that need new ductwork or attic access can run higher.

faqs.q: Do I need an HVAC dehumidifier if I have central air?
faqs.a: Not always. If your home stays at or below about 50% humidity all summer, your AC is doing the job. If it feels damp on mild days, the basement smells musty, or humidity regularly reads above 55–60%, a dedicated dehumidifier is worth it.

faqs.q: What size ducted dehumidifier do I need?
faqs.a: As a rough guide, 70–80 pints a day covers an average home in a humid climate, and 90–100 pints suits larger or leakier homes. A contractor should confirm sizing based on your climate, insulation and any damp basement or crawl space.
